newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland's pain recalled in "Tree" project.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland's pain recalled in "Tree" project.

text.p: It is called "an crann", the Irish for tree. Its roots are the violence that has tortured Northern Ireland and sprouted terms like "Bloody Sunday" and "Bloody Friday".
An Crann is a collection of memories of ordinary people scarred by the 27-year "troubles", which organiser Damian Gorman hopes will prevent fresh bloodshed in a still deeply divided province.

It is a collation of accounts by victims, relatives and bystanders in a war that has brought anguish to Protestants and Catholics alike and caused emptiness and grief in homes torn by a conflict that has killed more than 3,000.
"We are in a process of gathering a repository of these stories and holding them in some kind of trust," Gorman, one of Northern Ireland's best-known poet-playwrights, told Reuters.

"Nobody is barred from contributing their bit to this...It's in language that we don't often hear. That's what this project is about, that people might know by feeling what people beside them have been putting up with," he said in an interview.
"Their experience of loss -- it's vital for the rest of us to know about that because, in a sense, they are doing as individuals what we have to do as a community," Gorman said.
"They are going on living, with terrible things having happened to them," he said.

Sectarian hostility is increasing again after peace hopes bloomed but then faded when the Irish Republican Army (IRA), which draws support from Catholics, ended a 17-month truce and went back to war against British rule in the province.
A truce by pro-British Loyalist militants, extremists from the side of the Protestant majority, hangs by a thread.
THE TREE SPROUTS MANY BRANCHES
An Crann/The Tree, launched three years ago with a steering committee of Protestants and Catholics, has many branches.
It has sprouted more than 20 projects embracing writing, music, art and other activities that draw on community feeling. Eventually the results will be housed in a permanent centre.
To people who accuse him of simply turning over old ground, Gorman retorts that they don't know enough. "What I mean by that is we could slip back...into something terrible."
He feels that an understanding of past suffering might help block another descent into a pit of violence.
"If somebody is sitting down, speaking in the language of the heart, telling you what happened to them, you can't turn away from it," he said quietly.
A father tells of the horror of discovering his son has been blown to pieces by a bomb. "Why were we summoned by the police to views these remains? I do not know."
A woman recalls a guerrilla ambush on a car carrying her and two other teenagers. "I remember the bullets hitting me and lifting me off the seat.
"It seemed to go on forever...When it was all over, I could feel a burning pain all over my body...I was the only one of the wounded to survive."
Another tells how her unarmed brother was shot after rescuing a young boy struck by a plastic anti-riot bullet.
"He spied a soldier's helmet lying on the road and, being a person who loves souvenirs, he ran out to retrieve the helmet when the fatal shot rang out.
"The bullet went in at the top of his leg and hit a main artery, so with every beat of his heart he was pumping out blood."
YOUR FATHER IS DEAD
A girl writes of her devastation after an explosion. "My mother looked so sad and lonely. "It's alright,' I said to her. Someone told me that my daddy had injured his legs.
""No,' my mother said, "your daddy is dead.' My mind went blank and I took my youngest brother on my knee and started rocking with him..."No, no all this isn't true,' I burst out."
Some 4,000 contributions have been collated so far, many of them schoolchildren's letters to U.S.President Bill Clinton on the eve of a historic visit to Northern Ireland late in 1995.
"One thing I'll never forget is talking to a woman whose son was killed a long time ago," Gorman told Reuters.
"She said: "Obviously the absence is still there but the hardest thing of all for me to bear was that I was nobody's mother any more.'"
Across the province, towns and villages have dates circled in red as reminders of the carnage.
In Londonderry this weekend thousands will march to commemorate 13 unarmed Catholic nationalists shot dead by British troops during a street protest on January 30, 1972.
It became known as "Bloody Sunday".
NORTHERN IRELAND'S BLOODY ANNIVERSARIES
Belfast remembers especially "Bloody Friday", named for Friday, July 21, 1972, when the IRA detonated 26 bombs around the city centre, killing 11 people and injuring 130.
Like the victims of conflicts from Bosnia to Rwanda, the bereaved, the wounded and the eyewitnesses quietly shoulder a heavy burden of pain. But some are breaking their silence.
Memories can have healing powers, says Gorman.

"Our hope is that if people do say their own piece, in their own way, in their own time, because it will be from the heart it might resonate across all the divisions in a way that all the political chat, analysis and debate in the world does not."
